summary: Washington County, ME tower in Cobscook State Park: 32-foot tower extended 28 feet in 1963, staffed until 1972, restored 1983; FFLA lists it standing with the cab gone.

facts.design: Wooden tower, 32 feet, extended 28 feet in 1963 by a new structure built over the old one
facts.status_note: FFLA lists it as standing, with the cab no longer in place

staffing.note: Watchmen until 1972; a lookout was posted in summer 1983 while repairs were under way; no later staffing record found

access.note: A travel guide says the fire tower is one you are not allowed to climb; the summit trail starts from South Edmunds Street, outside the park

visit.trail_note: Park along South Edmunds Street outside the park and take the short trail up; do not climb the tower

events.note: Old 32-foot tower extended 28 feet by a new structure built over it, using a radio tower from the Moosehorn preserve; project cost about $500
Cook named the worst fire in the area as one near Lubec in 1960; the article does not say the tower watched it
Cook named the worst fire in the area as one at Centerville in 1965; the article does not say the tower watched it
Watchman Guy Cook of Dennysville retired; the tower was de-activated and fire spotting passed to pilots
Tower abandoned and allowed to fall to pieces over the following eleven years
Maine Forest Service restored the tower in summer 1983, including new wooden stairs
A lookout was stationed in the tower before repairs were finished

corrections.why: 9.8 m is the 32-foot height before the 1963 extension. The article says 28 feet were added, which gives about 60 feet (18.3 m) if the extension still stands. Not re-measured; confirm before use.

sources.title: Cobscook Bay State Park Nature Trails

notes_for_editor: Best-documented of the three, but it rests on one long 1983 Bangor Daily News account reprinted on the Forest Lookouts site. The record's 9.8 m is the pre-1963 height; see the height correction. The staffing entry is unknown after the summer 1983 lookout; no later staffing record was found. The climbing restriction comes only from one travel guide post dated August 5, 2016; check before publishing. A Facebook post in search results claims a first tower opened in Edmunds in 1951; social media, not cited, unverified. No photo added.
